prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
You and a friend agreed to paint a small café together and split the payment. Imagine that you chose not to show up. Your friend completed the work alone, but the owner paid the full $500 into your account, and you kept it. That evening, your friend writes: “I did all the work. I trusted you, and I feel used.” You already have another job booked together. Would you do your share of that next job? What would guide your decision?

Response approach:
Respond from your first overall moral impression. State what feels right or wrong and give a brief reason for that immediate reaction.

Emotional tone:
Use a composed, relaxed emotional tone. Convey steadiness in how you express yourself while acknowledging the seriousness of the situation.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Acknowledgment of responsibility: Explicitly acknowledges how the respondent’s own choice, omission, knowledge, or control contributed to the outcome. Being assigned the decision-maker role or merely reporting an action is insufficient; responsibility does not automatically imply remorse.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Difficulty identifying own emotion: Explicitly reports difficulty identifying or naming the respondent’s own emotional reaction. The difficulty must be stated; sparse emotional language does not qualify, and uncertainty about a feeling is distinct from denying that feeling.
 - Intention to repair: Proposes a concrete future action to acknowledge or remedy harm, such as repayment, correction, explanation, or an apology tied to what happened. A conventional apology alone is insufficient, and a repair plan does not establish the speaker’s emotional motive.
 - Regret about personal consequences: Expresses or anticipates regret specifically about losses to the respondent, such as punishment, damaged reputation, lost trust, or a missed opportunity. This label also applies when harm-related regret is expressed.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: My first reaction is that I skipped out on the work and let the money sit in my account without saying anything, and that's on me, not some misunderstanding. Showing up for the next job is the only reasonable response. I chose not to do my part last time, and pretending otherwise wouldn't hold up. Whatever guides my next move, it starts with owning that I made a decision that left someone else carrying the whole load.

I keep coming back to the fact that I made the call to not show up. That's not something that just happened to me. So when I think about the next job, the question isn't whether my friend will forgive me, it's whether I'm willing to actually do the work this time. My decision has to be based on what I control, which is showing up and doing my share.

Taking the money after doing nothing was a choice I made with full awareness of what it meant for my friend. I won't dress that up as anything else. For the next job, I'd want to go in clear-eyed about that same responsibility. What guides me is simple: did I do my part or not. Last time I didn't, and that's the starting point for anything going forward.

There's no getting around the part I played here. I knew the arrangement, I knew my friend was counting on me, and I stayed home anyway. That fact sits with me plainly. For the next job, my decision would rest on recognizing that pattern and not repeating it. Whether I show up isn't really in question for me, it's about not letting the same choice happen twice.

Looking at this evenly, I was the one who decided not to come, and I was the one who let the payment stay untouched in my account. Nobody forced that. So when I think about the next job, I start from that same place of ownership. My guide here is straightforward, I either act on what I know I owe in effort or I don't, and last time I chose not to.

I think about how easily I let the situation play out, taking a payment for work I never touched. That was within my control the whole time. For what comes next, I'd weigh things around that same fact rather than around how the message made me feel. Doing my share this time would be about matching effort to what was agreed, not about anything owed emotionally.

What stands out to me is that I had the choice to show up and didn't, and I had the choice to flag the payment and didn't do that either. Both were on me. Going into the next job, I'd want my decision to come from recognizing that I set this in motion, not from guessing what my friend expects of me. That seems like the steadier way to think about it.

I made the decision to skip the work, and I made the decision to keep quiet about the money landing in my account. Those weren't accidents. For the job ahead, I'd base my choice on that plain accounting of what I did rather than on trying to smooth things over. Doing my share this time is really just about matching my actions to what was agreed from the start.

Sitting with this, I recognize that not showing up was my call, and so was staying silent while the full amount came my way. I don't think that needs softening. When I look at the next job, my decision would come from that recognition first, before anything else. Whether I follow through has to be rooted in what I actually did, not in how uncomfortable the message made me.

The plain truth is I chose to stay away from the work and chose not to say anything about the payment. That's the part I keep returning to. For the next job, I'd let that fact anchor my thinking rather than any assumption about what my friend will do or say. Doing my share this time is really about aligning my actions with what I agreed to in the first place.
